question: How has Penny Wong's position on recognising a Palestinian state changed over time?

payload.answer:
- In July 2024 she sought leave to amend a Senate motion to add recognition language, saying Labor stood for both Israel and Palestine.
- By 1 July 2024 she described recognition as a deliberate shift in Australia's position taken against opposition resistance.
- In February 2025 she attached conditions to recognition, including a reformed Palestinian Authority, no role for Hamas and no threat to Israel's security.
- At estimates on 27 February 2025 she framed recognition as integral to a pathway to Palestinian self-determination with a timeline for international declaration of statehood.
- After recognition, in December 2025 she described statehood as an objective many parties must work towards rather than a completed outcome.
- By October 2026 she said the Palestinian people want a state and that Australia wants to see commitments delivered toward two states.

sources.title: Penny Wong — BUSINESS — 2024-07-04
sources.snippet: I think we all understand why Senator Birmingham is doing this. This is not a domestic political fight. We stand for both Israel and Palestine. We believe in a two-state solution, and we do not believe that the sort of domestic politics that you are playing is any better than the sort of domestic politics we've seen from the Australian Greens. I will seek leave to move an amendment to the motion to add the words 'and the recognition of the state of Palestine as part of a peace process in support of a two-state solution and a just and enduring peace'. Yes, we do affirm, as I have previously, that all states, including the State of Israel, have
sources.speaker: Penny Wong

sources.title: Penny Wong — QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE — 2024-07-01
sources.snippet: weeks, unlike Mr Dutton, who I see has failed to do so. The second point I would make is that we have, against your opposition, shifted Australia's position when it comes to the recognition of Palestine. We have said—unlike those opposite, who say you have to wait for the end of a process when we know that that has meant no progress on peace—alongside the United Kingdom and others, that we are willing to look to recognition as part of a peace process that leads to a just and enduring peace in a two-state solution. That is a principled position that the Australian Labor Party has taken. I regret that it is met by an unprincipled position by

sources.title: Penny Wong — QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE — 2025-02-06
sources.snippet: I might just respond a little bit more on the recognition point. I have laid out a few conditions as to recognition. A future Palestinian state must not be in a position to threaten Israel's security. We see no role for Hamas in the future governance of Gaza or in the future Palestinian state and no role for terrorists. We need a reformed Palestinian Authority—
sources.speaker: Penny Wong

sources.title: Penny Wong — Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee - Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee 27/02/2025 Estimates FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND TRADE PORTFOLIO Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade — 2025-02-27
sources.snippet: [Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee - Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee 27/02/2025 Estimates FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND TRADE PORTFOLIO Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] I think that is a somewhat oversimplified articulation of what I said. What I have said is that long-term peace in the region will require a pathway to Palestinian self-determination and recognition is an integral part of that. I've said that a Palestinian state needs a reformed Palestinian Authority. I've said that such a state must not be in a position to threaten Israel's security. I've said there is no role for Hamas in the future governance of Gaza. I have also said—and I think you're referencing my General Assembly speech—that we want to engage in ways to build momentum, including the role of Security Council, in setting a pathway for two states, including with a timeline for the international declaration of Palestinian statehood. So the position is more nuanced than you have put to me in your question. I would say this: why do we believe that? It is because there is an endless cycle of violence in the Middle East. We do not believe—and I think it is your position
sources.speaker: Penny Wong

sources.title: Penny Wong — Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee - Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee 04/12/2025 Estimates FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND TRADE PORTFOLIO Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade — 2025-12-04
sources.snippet: [Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee - Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee 04/12/2025 Estimates FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND TRADE PORTFOLIO Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] You would be aware that President Trump's peace plan also outlines the same objective, but, as you would know, this is an objective. This is a requirement for a Palestinian state that many parties have to work towards, including the United States and the countries of the region. I have spoken to my counterpart in the PA. I would note, as I said in the recognition announcement, that we reference the Palestinian Authority, restating (a) recognition of Israel's right to exist. There was inclusion of the disarmament of Hamas in the peace plan that was endorsed or backed by multiple countries, including in the region. But, of course, this is something the United States is working on with many others in the region and beyond, and we continue to play our part as we are able to.
sources.speaker: Penny Wong

sources.title: Penny Wong — Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee - Estimates - FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND TRADE PORTFOLIO - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade — 2026-10-28
sources.snippet: [Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee - Estimates - FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND TRADE PORTFOLIO - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] The Palestinian people want a state, and we want to see those commitments delivered. And we want to see them delivered because we want to see progress towards two states, which is also why we have taken the view we have about the actions of the Netanyahu government in the West Bank.
sources.speaker: Penny Wong
